notes.meaning: Jesus finished his farewell talk and then prayed out loud so his disciples could hear. Looking up to heaven was a sign of lifting his heart to God. "The hour" is the time God had set for his suffering and death. He asks the Father to "glorify" him, which means to honor him by carrying him through the cross and raising him again, so that he in turn could bring honor to the Father.

The Father gave the Son authority over all people. Jesus rules over everyone, but the purpose of that rule is to give eternal life to those the Father has given him. His power over the world serves the saving of his people.

differ.view: Those "given" to Christ are God's chosen people, the elect. Christ's kingdom reaches all people, but it brings salvation only to the chosen.
"Those given" means all believers, and this verse shows Christ meant his sacrifice to be for everyone. All people were placed in his hands so that all could have eternal life.

notes.meaning: Eternal life is knowing God and Jesus Christ, whom God sent. This knowing is more than facts in the head. It means love, trust and obedience. It begins now and will be made complete in heaven. "The only true God" sets God apart from false gods, not from Jesus, who is himself called the true God in 1 John 5:20.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that Jesus naming himself "Jesus Christ" is unusual in a prayer. They suggest it means "Jesus as the Christ," or that the words may be John's own explanation.

notes.meaning: Jesus honored the Father by finishing the work he was given. He speaks as if his death were already done, so his "finished work" includes the cross. His example teaches us to do the work God gives us faithfully, right to the end.

Jesus asks to return to the glory he shared with the Father before the world was made. This shows that he lived with God before creation and has always existed. He had set that glory aside during his humble life on earth. Now he asks for it to shine again.

God's "name" means his whole character. Jesus showed the disciples who God really is. These men belonged to the Father, and the Father gave them to Jesus to teach and send out. They were not perfect, but they held on to God's word.

differ.view: "They were Yours" points to God's choosing before time began. God counted them his own by free grace before they ever believed.
They were God's because he made them and because they came from Abraham's family. God gave them to Jesus by giving them faith in what he said.

notes.meaning: The disciples had come to see that everything Jesus had and taught came from the Father. Their knowledge was real, even if it was not yet complete. It is a comfort to know that all Christ is and does comes from God.

Jesus passed on the very words the Father gave him. The disciples welcomed those words. They knew for sure that he came from God, and they believed God sent him. Faith can know something surely even when it does not yet understand it fully.

Here Jesus prays for his disciples, not for "the world." In John, "world" here means people set against God. This does not mean he never prays for the world. He does so later in this prayer (v. 21) and on the cross.

differ.view: "The world" here means those God did not choose. In this prayer Christ pleads only for his chosen people. We still pray for everyone, because we cannot tell who is chosen.
Jesus leaves out the world only from these particular requests, which fit believers. He had simply not yet come to the part of the prayer where he prays for the world.

notes.meaning: Everything the Son has belongs to the Father, and everything the Father has belongs to the Son. No mere creature could say this. Only one equal with God could. Jesus says he is honored in his disciples, even with all their weaknesses.

Jesus is leaving, but his disciples must stay in a hostile world. He asks the "Holy Father" to keep them by his name. That means keeping them by his power and holding them in true knowledge of God and loyalty to him. He prays that they will be one, like the Father and Son. This is a likeness, not an equal oneness: one in heart, purpose and love.

While Jesus was with them, he guarded his disciples, and none was lost except Judas. "Son of destruction" means a man headed for ruin. Scripture had foretold the betrayal (Psalm 41:9). The prophecy did not force Judas to sin. It was given ahead of time so his fall would not shake the faith of others.

differ.view: Judas was never truly one of God's chosen. He only seemed to be because of his place among the apostles. So his loss does not overturn God's choosing.
Judas was one of those God gave to Jesus, yet he was lost. This shows such a giving was not unchangeable. Judas was lost because he would not be saved.

notes.meaning: Jesus prayed aloud in front of his disciples so they would hear him handing them into the Father's care. He wanted them to be filled with his joy. It is called his joy because it comes from him and rests on him.

Jesus gave the disciples God's word, and the world hated them for receiving it. They no longer belong to the world's way of thinking, just as Jesus does not. They live in the world, but they must not take their values from it.

Jesus does not ask God to take his followers out of the world. They had work to do, and the world needed their witness. He does not want them to run off and hide either. He asks God to keep them from "the evil one," Satan, and from sin, so they can face danger without being beaten.
Jesus repeats what he said in verse 14 for emphasis. His followers share his mind and spirit. The Spirit of God in true Christians is opposed to the spirit of the world.

To "sanctify" means to make holy and set apart for God. Jesus asks both that the disciples grow in holiness and that they be set apart for their work as his messengers. God uses his word, which is truth, to do this. Holiness keeps growing through the whole Christian life.
Just as the Father sent Jesus, Jesus sends his disciples into the world on the same mission. Because their task is so great, they need God's power to carry it out. Whom Christ sends, he stands by.

Jesus did not need to be made pure, since he had no sin. "I sanctify Myself" means he gave himself fully to his work, above all to offering himself as a sacrifice on the cross. His self-giving is the source of his people's holiness.

Jesus now prays for everyone who would ever believe through the apostles' message, so this prayer includes believers today. He asks that they be one, as the Father and Son are one. That means one in heart, purpose and love, which grows from being joined to God in Christ. Such unity helps the world believe, while quarrels among Christians are a stumbling block.

Jesus shares with believers the glory the Father gave him. This includes the honor of being God's children, loved by him, and the gift of his Spirit. He wants them to be "perfectly united," a unity that will only be complete in heaven. Their love for one another shows the world that God sent Jesus and loves believers as he loves his Son.

"I want" is a strong, earnest desire spoken by the Son with authority. Jesus asks that his people be with him in heaven and see his glory. Being with Christ and seeing him as he is will be the joy of heaven. The Father's love for him "before the foundation of the world" shows again that Jesus existed before creation.

Jesus calls on his "Righteous Father," because God's fairness stands behind bringing believers home. The world does not know God, but Jesus knows him fully. The disciples know that God sent Jesus, and through him they come to know the Father.

Jesus made God's name known, and he would keep doing so after his resurrection and through the Holy Spirit. His goal is that the Father's love for him would fill his people, and that Christ himself would live in them. The prayer ends on this note: "I in them."
